question: Gencoal S.A, headquartered in Vila do Conde and with share capital of EUR 2.8 million, produces mainly cured fish and seafood products. The cannery recently announced a mass redundancy affecting 97 workers, which became official on 2 April.

The company blames this mass redundancy – an anomaly in Portugal’s otherwise booming canning industry – on ‘supply chain disruption’, rising input costs, external competition and a fall in demand. Yet the President of the Vila do Conde Council says that just a few weeks ago, he met with the company and it had shown a ‘willingness to invest [...] and expand operations’.

There have been many reports in the national press about the nature of this mass redundancy; for example, the National Union of Workers in Food and Beverage Manufacturing (STIANOR) claims it is payback for recent strike action and comments from the trade union representative (one of the workers that has been laid off) describing his colleagues as ‘scared to speak out’ in the climate that has set in.
In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation? What does it have to say about the role that strike action plays in redundancies?
Does it know whether Gencoal S.A. has received EU funds? If so, please specify.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.5.2024) The Commission has knowledge of the mentioned redundancies, but it is not aware of the alleged causes for redundancy as presented in the question. On the role of strike, the functioning of national social dialogue falls under the responsibility of each Member State1.

The right to strike is a competence of the national authorities, including courts, to ensure that employers and national authorities correctly apply the national provisions and the fundamental rights resulting from their international obligations to respect workers’ rights. The Council Directive 98/59/EC2 contains procedural rules on collective dismissals.

It obliges employers to inform and consult workers when envisaging collective redundancies, and to notify the competent national authority. It does not harmonize the detailed rules for dismissals, nor does it prevent making individuals redundant. Portugal has transposed the Directive into national law by Articles 359-366 of the Labour Code, approved by Law no. 7/2009.

The company received EU funding from the European Fisheries Fund 2007-2013 (PROMAR) to support the modernisation of the company’s facilities and the last payment was made in 2015 for a total EU contribution of EUR 581 242,17.

The European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers3 may co-finance active labour market policy measures targeted to displaced workers and self-employed persons whose activity has ceased during major restructuring events if the conditions in Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2021/691 are met.

Similarly, the European Social Fund + can provide support for workers to improve their employability through training, upskilling and requalification, mainly through the Program Pessoas, Demografia, Qualificações e Inclusão4.
1 See art. 153(5) TFEU and Article 28 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. In addition,
